newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Serb hardliners confident of beating Plavsic.
newsitem.headline: Serb hardliners confident of beating Plavsic.

text.p: Hardline nationalists ignored President Biljana Plavsic's order to disband the Bosnian Serb parliament and went ahead on Friday with a session which will try to remove her from power.
Plavsic's dismissal was part of an agenda devoted to her conflict with the government and ex-president Radovan Karadzic who was driven from office last year as an indicted war criminal.

Karadzic's allies were confident they would be strong enough to force Plavsic to relinquish her authority to Vice President Draoljub Marjanic, but parliamentary sources said the meeting might last into the weekend before a vote was taken.
The hardliners claimed the support of Serbia's President Slobodan Milosevic who has been rebuilding links with the Karadzic faction since making them embrace the 1995 peace agreement in Bosnia.
But any attempt to topple Plavsic would put them on a collision course with international mediators implementing the agreement who have endorsed her constitutional authority.
Plavsic, who accused the nationalists of corrupting the government and obstructing peace, dissolved parliament on Thursday and set new elections for September 1.
She was supported on Friday by 7,000 demonstrators who gathered outside her office in the northern town of Banja Luka and urged her not to back down.
"I'm sorry this happened but crime must be stopped," Plavsic told them. "(War) victims did not fall for a state of thieves but for a state of honest people."
Representatives of the United Nations and Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) in Sarajevo warned the hardliners that they would not recognise decisions taken by parliament.

Simon Haselock, spokesman for the U.N. High Representative in Bosnia, told reporters: "Since the assembly has been dissolved, anything that meets this afternoon cannot be considered an assembly meeting."
He added: "Clearly the international community will deal only with constitutionally recognised bodies. But we still have to see what happens in the next 24 hours. That will be crucial."
Western mediators made clear that efforts to rebuild Bosnia on the basis of the Dayton peace agreement were at a turning point.

A diplomat in Sarajevo said: "If we are willing to see the one person in power in Republika Srpska (Serb Republic) who is willing to carry out the peace agreement be crushed by an indicted war criminal, where are we?"
Karadzic's prospects of forcing the parliament to do his bidding improved when the 14-strong block of legislators from the Moslem SDA party decided not to attend.
Without their votes, it was unlikely that members of the ruling SDS who support Plavsic would be strong enough to prevent the hardliners getting their way.

By making public allegations of corruption against named government leaders and shedding light on Karadzic's illegal influence, Plavsic may have dealt a possibly crippling blow to the Bosnian Serb wartime leadership.
Karadzic aide Jovan Zametica told reporters in Pale: "I am not ready to say that we have a consititutional crisis but we definitely have a political crisis."
The independent Belgrade news agency Beta quoted Plavsic as saying she feared her life might be in danger as a result of her revelations.
She alleged that three members of Bosnian Serb state security forces who were found in a room opposite her office on Thursday were monitoring her movements.
